title: Vampire Planet: Of Ecocide and Empire
author: Joshua Frank
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Screen-
Shot-2026-08-27-at-12.46.35-PM-680x457.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/28/vampire-
planet-ecocide-and-empire/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Screen-
Shot-2026-08-27-at-12.46.35-PM-680x457.png)

Fire at the Shahran Oil Depot in northwestern Tehran following an Israeli
airstrike on March 7th, one of several facilities struck in the vicinity while
around thirty oil storage and processing sites were attacked across the
country. Source: @sentdefender

When we talk about war, it’s usually in numbers. Innocents and soldiers
killed. Bombs dropped. Money spent. We hear figures like [7.6
million](https://www.theatlantic.com/international/2026/06/us-iran-war-air-
strikes/687664/) and [37.5 billion](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-
east/us-war-iran-has-cost-375-billion-so-far-pentagon-says-2026-07-21/). There
are so many like this that they often feel meaningless, even with context. In
this case, 7.6 million is the tonnage of bombs the US has dropped on Iran, and
37.5 billion, the cost of this illegal war.

Intentionally or not, large numbers like these obscure the reality of war’s
toll.

The number of victims of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, for instance, doesn’t do
justice to the violence Gazans have been forced to endure.

Likewise, the number of bombs dropped and dollars spent in an attempt to
destroy Iran’s government says nothing about the true human and environmental
costs of US/Israel aggression. It reduces these crimes to statistics that
don't accurately convey the horror on the ground, and so much of the ground in
the Middle East is soaked with the pollution and blood of
empire.[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Screen-
Shot-2026-08-21-at-11.06.12-AM.png)](https://www.pilsencommunitybooks.com/item/UfU8gx4LO98oZP-
hvrl3zQ)

The US has a long history of waging war on ecologies in the Middle East,
dating back to at least Operation Desert Storm in 1991.

The aftermath of the US's massive bombing campaigns in Iraq was tangible.
[Poisoned aquifers](https://insideclimatenews.org/news/29122021/iraq-
ecocide/). Widespread [contamination of
soil](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2010/jan/22/iraq-nuclear-contaminated-
sites) with depleted uranium and other toxic metals. [Air
pollution](https://www.apha.org/policy-and-advocacy/public-health-policy-
briefs/policy-database/2015/12/16/08/56/cleanup-of-us-military-burn-pits-in-
iraq-and-afghanistan) from scorched oil infrastructure. Irreparable [damage to
marine ecosystems](https://nautil.us/revisiting-the-environmental-ruin-of-the-
first-gulf-war-1279095).

Saddam, too, was guilty of committing ecocidal acts. He deliberately
[drained](http://worldwateratlas.org/narratives/marsh/marshes-in-the-river-
tigres-and-euphrates-dried-up/) the ecologically significant Mesopotamian
marshlands in southern Iraq, and Iraqi soldiers [set fire to oil
fields](https://adst.org/2016/04/towering-infernos-the-kuwait-oil-fires/) as
they fled Kuwait.

Yes, wars are inherently environmentally disastrous, and, on a global scale,
the US is far more culpable than most - from nuclear detonations to Agent
Orange. The US/Israeli bombardment of Iran today is a continuation of this
belligerence.

We know, from Hegseth’s admission to Congress, how many targets have been hit
and how much money has been spent. But what we don’t truly know, and perhaps
won’t for many years to come, is what these bombs and munitions have inflicted
on the people and land of Iran.

What we already can gather from the US bombing of Iran: The US and Israel have
targeted oil infrastructure, releasing millions of tons of [greenhouse
gases](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/oiRgyIWWdtY), which in turn have created
toxic, [acidic rain](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/mar/19/down-
to-earth-iran-us-israeli-war-environmental-destruction) clouds. Bombing near
coastal regions has caused oil spills, and slicks are drifting into
[biologically important](https://theconversation.com/iran-oil-spill-the-war-
is-leaving-environmental-scars-that-ceasefires-cannot-heal-286407) island
ecosystems.

And, if Iraq serves as a guide, there’s sure to be severe soil and groundwater
contamination that will plague Iranians for [decades to
come](https://ceobs.org/operation-epic-fury-emerging-environmental-harm-and-
risks-in-iran-and-the-region/). It’s difficult to grasp the toll the US war
machine continues to inflict, not only on people but also on the ecosystems we
depend on for survival.

In their must-see film, [_Earth’s Greatest
Enemy_](https://earthsgreatestenemy.com/), Abby Martin and Mike Prsyner
explore this toll beyond mere numbers. In an emotional and gripping narrative,
they explain the scale of the US military machine and its ongoing
destructiveness to our burning planet. Ed Rampell wrote a (well-deserved)
[glowing review](https://www.counterpunch.org/2025/09/14/abby-martins-new-
film-exposes-earths-greatest-enemy/) for us last spring.

This week, they released a deleted scene from the film, which is now available
to stream.

If you want to begin to understand just how devastating the US empire was and
remains, I implore you to watch the film and share it with everyone who still
believes in the version of America that Donald Trump wants taught in our
schools.

+++

A startling [study](https://dmscdn.vuelio.co.uk/publicitem/30a7d43a-355a-4fff-
ba7d-0d615d39c9c0) released in July reveals that the carbon footprint of metal
production is 10 times higher than previously thought, largely because acid-
laden runoff reacts with oxygen-rich surface waters and releases a large
amount of carbon. This is sour news for those hoping we can mine our way out
of this climate crisis.

As images of a horrific, deadly flood fill our news feeds, it’s [becoming
clear](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/27/world/asia/nepal-flood-cause-
landslide-glacier-collapse.html) that our warming climate played a role in
dislodging an enormous glacier, triggering a massive mudslide on the Nepal-
Tibet border this week that killed hundreds. The deluge of rock and water
registered as a 5.2 geological event, equivalent to 1,000 tons of TNT.

The Himalayas contain 15,000 large glaciers, and nearly all of them are
receding fast, creating conditions in which huge amounts of ice can break off,
essentially slicing off the sides of entire mountains. They are expected to
lose [70%](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/himalayan-glaciers-
track-lose-up-75-ice-by-2100-report-2023-06-20/) of their ice by 2100. Nepal
emits less than 0.1% of global emissions but is one of the most vulnerable
countries to the wrath of climate chaos as glaciers melt.

It’s almost certain that many natural disasters (if you can call them that)
will occur in the Himalayas, crushing more communities as our climate
continues to warm.

+++
